parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from absorbēns (“absorbing”) + -ia (“abstract noun suffix”), equivalent to absorbente + -ia. Absorbentia exists as a real word in Latin, but only as a form of the participle absorbēns. Doublet of absorbancia, a partial calque of English absorbancy. Cognate with Catalan absor
Borrowed from Latin ācta (“register of events”), plural of āctum, from agō. Sense 4 is borrowed from English act.
Inherited from Late Latin cocīnāre, from Latin coquīnāre. The slang sense is a semantic loan from English cook.
Borrowed from Latin corpus, possibly through the intermediate of English corpus, according to the RAE. Doublet of the inherited cuerpo.
From Latin quartus. Doublet of cuarta. The sense of room is after a common division of houses (4 or 5 sections). As a unit of English measure, calque of English quart. Compare English quarter.
Borrowed from Latin quaestiōnem. Sense 2 is a semantic loan from English question.
By surface analysis, evento + -al. Ultimately based off Latin ēventuālis. The "eventual", "happening eventually" sense is a semantic loan from English eventual.
From Latin fēmina (“woman, female”) + -cidio, on the pattern of English femicide, by analogy with homicidio.

Pseudo-Latinism, derived from idem (“same”) + potentia (“the quality of having power”), coined as a calque of English idempotence, equivalent to ídem + potencia. Cognate with Catalan idempotència, French idempotence, Italian idempotenza, Portuguese idempotência, and Romanian idempotență.

parole.significato: English or American pound avoirdupois (a unit of mass equivalent to 453.6 g)
parole.testo: From Latin libra (“Roman pound, scale”). Doublet of lira. In reference to the English unit, a calque of English pound. Cognate with Galician and Portuguese libra and Catalan lliura.

parole.significato: English or American mile (a unit of distance equivalent to about 1.6 km)
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin mīlia (“Roman mile”), plural of mīlle (“thousand”) in reference to its composition of a thousand Roman paces. In reference to the English unit, calqued from English mile. Cognate with Catalan milla and Portuguese milha.

Borrowed from New Latin potassium, from English potassium, coined in 1807 by Humphrey Davy, from English potash, from Dutch potasch, from Middle Dutch pottaschen (literally “pot ashes”), ultimately derived from Proto-Germanic *puttaz (“pot”) and *askǭ (“ash”).
Borrowed from New Latin sodium, from Italian soda, coined by H. Davy, 1778-1829, British physicist and chemist who discovered it.
